paragraphs: Reading text in video involves following text across changing frames and handling different orientations and settings. This paper introduces BOVText, a bilingual benchmark intended to broaden evaluation beyond the single languages and narrow scenarios common in earlier datasets. It contains more than 1,850 videos and 1.6 million frames, spanning over 30 categories.

The annotations distinguish text with different roles, including titles, captions, and text appearing within scenes. That distinction makes the benchmark useful for studying more than whether letters are visible: it also records how text functions within a video. Its range of settings includes everyday video logs, driving footage, and movies.

The paper also introduces TransVTSpotter, an end-to-end Transformer framework. It uses object features from the previous frame as queries to track text in the current frame, and predicts rotation angles to accommodate differently oriented text. On ICDAR2015 video, the authors report state-of-the-art performance of 44.2% MOTA at 13 frames per second. That result supports the proposed method on the named benchmark, alongside the broader dataset contribution.
neurips-2021-a-bilingual-openworld-video.tldr: BOVText expands bilingual video-text evaluation, while TransVTSpotter uses information across frames and rotation prediction to spot and track text.

paragraphs: ATOM3D addresses a practical obstacle to learning from molecular structure: researchers lacked both systematic benchmarks and a unified toolkit for working with three-dimensional molecular data. The paper assembles new and existing datasets covering several major classes of biomolecules, creating a shared basis for evaluating methods across different molecular problems.

The authors implement several kinds of learning methods that use three-dimensional structure. Across the evaluated tasks, these methods consistently improve performance over approaches using one- or two-dimensional representations. The findings indicate that spatial information can contribute useful predictive information in these settings, supporting further investigation of molecular learning that explicitly represents geometry.

Architecture also matters. Three-dimensional convolutional networks excel on tasks involving complex geometries, graph networks perform well where detailed positional information is needed, and equivariant networks show promise. These are task-dependent findings rather than a single architecture winning everywhere. The accompanying Python package provides tools for processing datasets, training models, and evaluating results, making it easier to reproduce comparisons and investigate the substantial room for improvement identified by the authors.
neurips-2021-atom3d-tasks-on-molecules-i.tldr: ATOM3D benchmarks molecular learning and finds consistent benefits from three-dimensional representations, with architecture choice affecting performance across tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian deep learning aims to make neural networks express how uncertain their predictions are. This matters for safety-critical applications, where confidence needs to be reliable as well as predictions accurate. The paper argues that commonly used experimental settings do not adequately reflect the complexities of the real applications that most need trustworthy uncertainty estimates.

The RETINA Benchmark addresses this mismatch using two publicly available collections of high-resolution retinal images showing different degrees of diabetic retinopathy. The authors turn these data into automated diagnosis tasks designed to require reliable uncertainty quantification. They assess established and newer Bayesian methods using evaluation measures tailored to the tasks.

The contribution includes implementations, reproducible benchmarking software, and a substantial experimental reference: 400 hyperparameter configurations, evaluation with at least six random seeds each, and computation spanning 100 TPU days and 20 GPU days. This provides a concrete setting for comparing how methods handle uncertainty in medically relevant prediction tasks. The abstract establishes the benchmark and experimental scope without identifying a method that resolves the reliability problem.
neurips-2021-benchmarking-bayesian-deep-.tldr: RETINA benchmarks Bayesian deep learning on retinal-image diagnosis tasks designed to test predictive uncertainty under realistic complexities.

paragraphs: When several learning agents must cooperate, comparing algorithms is difficult if researchers use different tasks, evaluation criteria, or implementation choices. This paper tackles that problem through a systematic comparison across a diverse set of cooperative tasks. Its aim is to provide reference results and clarify how different approaches behave across learning settings.

The evaluation covers three classes of methods: independent learning, centralized multi-agent policy gradients, and value decomposition. Considering these classes together broadens the comparison beyond variants of one approach. The experiments establish expected performance on the studied tasks and provide insights into the effectiveness of different ways of organizing cooperative learning.

The authors also release EPyMARL, extending the existing PyMARL codebase with additional algorithms and flexible implementation settings, including parameter sharing. This makes such choices explicit parts of experimentation. Two additional environments focus on coordination when rewards are sparse, creating tasks where useful feedback is limited. Together, the evaluations, configurable software, and environments supply practical infrastructure for more comparable research into how agents learn to work together.
neurips-2021-benchmarking-multi-agent-de.tldr: The paper compares three major cooperative multi-agent learning approaches and releases configurable software and environments for more consistent evaluation.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations suggest changes to an individual's features that could lead a model to produce a favorable outcome. For example, an explanation might suggest increasing income to obtain insurance approval. Choosing a suitable explanation method matters because these outputs are intended to inform action, and researchers have proposed many competing approaches.

The paper identifies an obstacle to meaningful comparison: available implementations can shape method selection more than a systematic assessment of alternatives. CARLA addresses this by bringing counterfactual explanation methods into a shared Python library. It benchmarks 11 popular methods across different datasets and predictive models, with integrated evaluation measures.

The resulting framework supports both comparisons of existing approaches and research on future methods. Standardized datasets and measures give researchers common reference points when assessing explanations, while released experimental results provide baselines for subsequent work. The central contribution is therefore an accessible comparison infrastructure. It helps researchers examine which method fits a setting instead of relying mainly on whichever implementation happens to be readily available.
neurips-2021-carla-a-python-library-to-b.tldr: CARLA provides a shared Python framework for comparing 11 counterfactual explanation methods across datasets, models, and standardized evaluation measures.

paragraphs: CodeNet provides a large collection of programs for research on using AI to support software development. It contains more than 14 million code samples, approximately 500 million lines, and 55 programming languages. This breadth makes it a resource for studying multiple coding tasks within one collection, including tasks relevant to modernizing existing software.

The dataset includes annotations supporting code classification, similarity assessment, translation between programming languages, and improvements to runtime or memory use. These are different aspects of software quality and functionality, so the contribution extends beyond generating code. Preprocessing tools also convert source programs into representations that machine learning models can use.

Sample inputs and expected outputs are available for 98.5% of the code samples. They provide a way to check program behavior and could potentially supply feedback for reinforcement learning aimed at improving code quality. The paper reports classification and similarity experiments as reference results. Its main contribution is the scale and organization of the research resource, with the other supported tasks representing opportunities for further work.
neurips-2021-codenet-a-large-scale-ai-fo.tldr: CodeNet supplies millions of annotated programs across 55 languages to support research on code understanding, translation, and performance improvement.

paragraphs: CodeXGLUE creates a shared benchmark for machine learning methods that understand or generate programs. The paper treats evaluation infrastructure as a way to accelerate research: new methods need datasets on which to learn and common settings in which their results can be compared. It brings these resources together for a range of programming-language problems.

The collection covers 10 tasks across 14 datasets and includes a platform for model evaluation and comparison. Organizing several tasks within one benchmark gives researchers a broader setting for developing and validating methods. Its scope includes both interpreting existing code and producing code, reflecting distinct goals within machine learning for programming.

To make the platform easier to use, the authors provide three baseline systems based on BERT-style, GPT-style, and encoder-decoder models. These supply starting implementations and reference approaches for subsequent experiments. The paper's contribution is this combination of data, evaluation support, and baseline systems. Together, they provide practical foundations for testing proposed methods across the program understanding and generation problems represented in the benchmark.
neurips-2021-codexglue-a-machine-learnin.tldr: CodeXGLUE combines 10 programming tasks, 14 datasets, an evaluation platform, and three baseline model families for code understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that describe data. This paper introduces a reproducible, open-source platform for comparing methods, addressing a lack of consistent evaluation standards. The study evaluates 14 symbolic regression methods and seven machine learning methods across 252 regression problems, giving the comparison substantial variety.

The benchmark separates two goals. On real-world datasets, where the underlying equation is unknown, it evaluates whether methods produce models with low prediction error and low complexity. On synthetic problems with known equations, including physics equations and differential-equation systems, it tests whether methods can recover the exact expression under different amounts of noise.

Within these experiments, the strongest real-world methods combine genetic algorithms with parameter estimation, semantic search guidance, or both. For exact equation recovery in noisy data, deep learning and genetic algorithm approaches perform similarly. These findings depend on the evaluated tasks and goals, highlighting why prediction quality and equation recovery deserve separate assessment. Reproduction instructions and support for adding methods make the platform a basis for continued comparison.
neurips-2021-contemporary-symbolic-regre.tldr: A broad symbolic regression benchmark finds task-dependent strengths, with hybrid genetic methods leading real-world regression in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Manipulating objects that bend and change shape presents challenges beyond controlling rigid objects. This paper introduces environments involving highly deformable objects with nontrivial topology. The tasks emphasize three-dimensional motion in which gravity and inertia have meaningful effects, making dynamic behavior a central part of the learning problem.

The environments support tasks of different complexity and include variants with procedurally generated cloth objects and randomized material textures. Users can import objects and textures or change object size and material properties. These options let researchers vary the objects and conditions involved while working within the same experimental infrastructure.

Fast execution, parallel data generation, and compatibility with the OpenAI Gym interface are intended to make experimentation accessible to reinforcement learning researchers. The authors also frame the environments as a meeting point for several fields: vision and machine learning for processing complex inputs, graphics and topology for developing representations, and robotics for learning control. The contribution is a customizable set of dynamic challenges designed to support that combined research effort.
neurips-2021-dynamic-environments-with-d.tldr: The paper provides customizable simulation environments for learning to control deformable objects in three-dimensional tasks shaped by gravity and inertia.

paragraphs: Off-policy policy evaluation is an important reinforcement learning problem, particularly for applications where evaluating a decision-making method has safety implications. The paper responds to a growing number of proposed evaluation methods by creating an experimental benchmark and an empirical study. Its central motivation is the need for standardized comparisons as interest in deploying learning-based systems increases.

The study emphasizes diversity in experimental design. The benchmarking suite is built to stress-test methods and investigate how different experimental attributes interact to affect performance. This focus matters because a method's empirical behavior can depend on the conditions under which it is assessed. Examining those interactions is therefore part of the benchmark's purpose.

The authors turn their experimental findings into practical guidelines for off-policy evaluation and release the Caltech OPE Benchmarking Suite, or COBS, as open-source software. The contribution joins reusable evaluation infrastructure with guidance derived from experiments. By inviting further contributions, the benchmark also provides a shared starting point for researchers who want to extend the empirical comparison of these methods.
neurips-2021-empirical-study-of-off-poli.tldr: COBS provides diverse experiments for stress-testing off-policy evaluation methods and distills the resulting evidence into practical guidance.

paragraphs: APPS evaluates whether a model can turn a natural-language programming specification into satisfactory Python code. The benchmark contains 10,000 problems, ranging from exercises with one-line solutions to substantial algorithmic challenges. This variety is intended to assess coding ability across a broader range of difficulty than more restricted code-generation settings.

Generated programs are evaluated using test cases, connecting the assessment to what the code actually does. The authors fine-tune large language models using GitHub data and the benchmark's training set. They report that syntax errors become exponentially less prevalent as models improve, suggesting progress in producing code that follows the language's formal rules.

Functional success remains more limited in the reported experiments: models such as GPT-Neo pass approximately 20% of test cases on introductory problems. This is a test-case result, rather than a claim that 20% of complete problems are solved. The findings indicate emerging coding ability while leaving substantial scope for improvement. APPS provides a common behavioral measure for tracking such progress across programming challenges.
neurips-2021-measuring-coding-challenge-.tldr: APPS tests generated Python programs on 10,000 coding problems, finding emerging functional ability alongside substantial remaining difficulty.

paragraphs: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems designed to measure mathematical problem solving in machine learning models. Each problem includes a complete worked solution. These solutions make the dataset useful for teaching models to produce derivations and explanations, as well as for evaluating their answers.

The authors also contribute a large auxiliary pretraining dataset intended to teach mathematical fundamentals. Their experiments improve accuracy on MATH, but performance remains relatively low even for very large Transformer models. The results therefore identify a demanding evaluation setting in which the tested models still struggle despite additional training resources and substantial model size.

The paper's scaling conclusion is conditional: if the observed trends continue, increasing computation budgets and parameter counts alone would be impractical for achieving strong mathematical reasoning. It does not establish that scaling can never help. Instead, the authors argue that new algorithmic advances will likely be needed. The benchmark and worked solutions provide concrete resources for investigating approaches that improve mathematical reasoning under those challenges.
neurips-2021-measuring-mathematical-prob.tldr: MATH supplies challenging mathematics problems with worked solutions and finds that the observed scaling trends make strong reasoning through scaling alone appear impractical.

paragraphs: Model quantization is used to accelerate neural-network inference, but an algorithm's reported performance may not translate cleanly into a reproducible, deployable system. This paper attributes that gap to inconsistent training procedures and insufficient attention to hardware requirements. MQBench brings those two issues into the evaluation of quantization methods.

The benchmark compares advanced quantization algorithms under a unified training pipeline and considers deployment on CPUs, GPUs, ASICs, and DSPs. This connects the algorithmic comparison to the platforms on which models are intended to run. The shared training procedure also makes it possible to reassess apparent differences between methods under aligned experimental conditions.

With training settings aligned, the authors find roughly similar performance among existing algorithms on the conventional academic track. Hardware-deployable quantization, however, shows a large accuracy gap, and no evaluated algorithm wins every MQBench challenge. These findings suggest that academic comparisons alone do not settle practical method selection. Reproducibility and hardware compatibility expose important dimensions of performance that require further work.
neurips-2021-mqbench-towards-reproducibl.tldr: MQBench finds similar academic performance under aligned training settings but substantial accuracy challenges when quantization must satisfy hardware deployment requirements.

paragraphs: Machine learning benchmarks are most useful when their results can be interpreted, compared, and reproduced. This paper advocates curated collections of tasks that standardize how benchmarks are set up, run, and reported. It supplies software within OpenML to make those collections practical resources for researchers conducting algorithm evaluations.

The tools are accessible through Python, Java, and R, using standardized data formats, interfaces, and client libraries. Each suite includes extensive information about its datasets. Suites can also be shared and reused in later studies, allowing researchers to build comparisons around an established collection instead of assembling a new experimental setup for every project.

As a concrete example, the authors introduce OpenML-CC18, a carefully curated classification benchmark suite. They discuss use cases and applications demonstrating the utility of the suite and the broader tooling. The contribution centers on making benchmark organization itself reusable: task collections, associated information, and software access become shared components of research. This supports more consistent evaluation practices across studies using the same benchmark resources.
neurips-2021-openml-benchmarking-suites-.tldr: OpenML benchmarking suites package curated tasks, dataset information, and reusable tools to support consistent and reproducible algorithm comparisons.

paragraphs: RadGraph turns information in chest X-ray reports into structured entities and relationships. The authors design an information extraction schema and release expert annotations for training and evaluation. This structure makes report content available for computational research that needs more than an unorganized passage of clinical text.

The development data contain radiologist annotations for 500 MIMIC-CXR reports. The test data contain two independent expert annotation sets for 100 reports, divided equally between MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert. A trained deep learning model achieves relation-extraction micro F1 scores of 0.82 and 0.73 on the respective test sets, providing a reference for how well the schema can be extracted automatically.

The authors then apply the model at much larger scale, producing annotations for 220,763 MIMIC-CXR reports and 500 CheXpert reports, with links to corresponding chest images. These larger annotations are model-generated, distinct from the expert-labeled development and test data. The combined resource supports medical language research and, through the image mappings, research connecting radiology text with visual information.
neurips-2021-radgraph-extracting-clinica.tldr: RadGraph provides expert-labeled and automatically extracted entities and relations from chest X-ray reports, with links supporting text-and-image research.

paragraphs: Models deployed for long periods encounter changes that short datasets may not capture. This paper introduces the Long-term Thermal Drift dataset to study that problem in thermal surveillance. It covers one location over eight months and includes information about weather, day and night, and activity in the scene.

The authors use these accompanying variables to examine relationships between environmental conditions and the performance of selected object- and anomaly-detection algorithms. Long-term performance is most strongly correlated with temperature, humidity, the day/night cycle, and scene activity. This suggests prioritizing coverage of those variables when collecting data for similar applications; the stated correlations alone do not establish that each variable causes the performance changes.

The paper also proposes a baseline response to drift: detect when a change occurs, collect additional data at that point, and retrain the models. This improves subsequent performance by an average of 25% across the tested algorithms. The result provides evidence for this adaptation strategy within the study's thermal-imaging setting, while the dataset enables further examination of changes over time.
neurips-2021-seasons-in-drift-a-long-ter.tldr: An eight-month thermal dataset links model performance to environmental changes and shows benefits from collecting new data and retraining after detected drift.

paragraphs: Distributional shift occurs when the data a model faces differ from those underlying its development. The Shifts Dataset supports evaluation of robustness and uncertainty estimates under such changes. The paper responds to a gap between the many proposed methods and the more limited availability of large, standardized benchmarks for assessing them.

The dataset draws on industrial sources and services and includes three tasks: weather prediction with tabular data, machine translation, and vehicle motion prediction for self-driving cars. Each task contains real distributional shifts. Together, they broaden evaluation beyond the small regression and image-classification settings that the authors identify as common in earlier work.

This diversity matters because the tasks require different kinds of outputs, including structured predictions, and use substantially different input information. A common dataset collection allows uncertainty and robustness methods to be examined across these practical settings. The paper describes the data and supplies baseline results for every task. Its contribution is a foundation for evaluating methods under naturally occurring changes across multiple modalities, rather than only within one familiar task type.
neurips-2021-shifts-a-dataset-of-real-di.tldr: Shifts provides industrial data and baselines for evaluating uncertainty and robustness under real changes in weather, translation, and vehicle-motion prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods attempt to explain predictions by assigning importance to input features. Comparing these explanations is difficult: human evaluations can be needed, and quantitative measures on real-world data may demand extensive data or computation. XAI-BENCH addresses this evaluation problem through synthetic datasets and a library for benchmarking attribution methods.

The key advantage of the synthetic setting is that conditional expected values can be computed efficiently. These quantities support the calculation of ground-truth Shapley values and other evaluation measures, providing reference information against which explanations can be assessed. The datasets expose configurable parameters so researchers can construct varied settings intended to resemble aspects of real-world data.

The authors demonstrate the library by comparing popular explanation techniques across multiple measures and settings. This makes the resource useful for investigating how an explanation method behaves as the evaluation conditions change. The contribution is a controllable, computationally efficient experimental foundation for explainability research. It addresses the difficulty of obtaining evaluation references while retaining flexibility in the types of synthetic data used.
neurips-2021-synthetic-benchmarks-for-sc.tldr: XAI-BENCH uses configurable synthetic data to make reference attribution values and other explanation-quality measures efficient to compute.

paragraphs: Self-supervised speech learning uses unlabeled recordings to learn representations that can support later tasks. LeBenchmark addresses the difficulty of comparing these models consistently, especially outside English. It provides an open-source, reproducible framework focused on French speech, combining documented, varied speech corpora with seven pretrained wav2vec 2.0 models.

The evaluation covers speech recognition, spoken language understanding, speech translation, and emotion recognition. Shared protocols and scoring scripts make those different uses part of an organized assessment. This breadth matters because the usefulness of a speech representation is examined across several kinds of downstream work rather than being judged through one task alone.

The authors compare two ways of using pretrained models: keeping them frozen or fine-tuning them for a particular task. This explicitly distinguishes the value of a fixed representation from performance after task-specific adaptation. They report state-of-the-art results on most of the French tasks considered. Alongside those results, the released models, data resources, and evaluation setup provide a reproducible basis for developing and comparing further speech-learning methods.
neurips-2021-task-agnostic-and-task-spec.tldr: LeBenchmark standardizes French speech evaluation across four tasks and compares frozen versus fine-tuned self-supervised models.

paragraphs: Search-based tensor compilers turn mathematical operations into fast low-level programs by exploring alternative implementations. Measuring every candidate directly on hardware takes time, so a cost model predicts performance and helps guide the search. TenSet provides data for learning those predictions, addressing the lack of a standard resource for pretraining and comparing learned cost models.

The dataset contains 52 million program-performance records collected from six hardware platforms. The paper also studies choices involved in building and evaluating cost models, including data collection, model architecture, training losses, transfer learning, and evaluation measures. This connects the dataset to the practical decisions researchers face when using it.

A cost model pretrained on TenSet speeds up search in the evaluated state-of-the-art tensor compiler by as much as tenfold. The reported gain concerns the time spent finding implementations, rather than a tenfold increase in the execution speed of the resulting programs. The result shows that learning from a large performance dataset can substantially reduce compiler search costs in the demonstrated setting.
neurips-2021-tenset-a-large-scale-progra.tldr: TenSet supplies 52 million performance records, enabling a pretrained cost model to accelerate tensor-compiler search by up to tenfold.

paragraphs: Abusive-language detection needs suitable training and evaluation data, but large, carefully annotated non-English collections have been scarce or inaccessible. This paper releases German news-comment datasets to address that gap. The authors describe them as the largest annotated German abusive-language comment datasets available at the time of the work.

The resource includes decisions made by professional moderators and annotations from a thorough crowd-based study. These two sources of labeling bring both moderation decisions and additional structured annotation into the published data. The authors emphasize this annotation effort as a way to achieve a high labeling standard for research on abusive comments.

The study compares baseline algorithms with advanced Transformer language models fine-tuned on the new datasets and an existing alternative. It also cross-evaluates their performance, extending the analysis beyond a single dataset's internal results. The contribution combines public data, an explicit annotation effort, and empirical model comparisons. Together, these provide resources for investigating automated detection of abusive German comments in a domain where access to well-curated data has been a barrier.
neurips-2021-texttt-rp-mod-texttt-rp-cro.tldr: RP-Mod and RP-Crowd provide German abusive-comment datasets combining professional moderation decisions, crowd annotations, and comparative model evaluations.

paragraphs: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy offers a non-intrusive way to measure brain activity, but its signals differ substantially between people. That variation makes it difficult to build brain-computer interfaces for new users without collecting extensive individual training data. The Tufts dataset targets this problem of generalizing mental-workload prediction across participants.

It contains recordings from 68 people, with segments labeled at four workload levels. Participants performed controlled n-back tasks to induce different working-memory demands. The accompanying training and evaluation protocol is designed to assess generalization fairly while preventing overlap or leakage between training and test data, making future results more comparable.

Using this benchmark, the authors show that models trained on abundant recordings from other participants can effectively classify a new person's data, reducing calibration and setup time. Performance improves as the available dataset grows. The study also examines error rates across key subpopulations to audit equity concerns. These findings support collecting and sharing multi-participant data as a practical route toward interfaces that transfer more effectively to new users.
neurips-2021-the-tufts-fnirs-mental-work.tldr: The Tufts benchmark shows that shared fNIRS data from many participants can support mental-workload classification for new users with less calibration.

paragraphs: Lifelong language learning asks a model to learn tasks sequentially while retaining earlier abilities. Evaluating this is difficult when benchmarks cover only newly added classes or mix incompatible task setups. The paper identifies a benchmark that combines multi-label and multi-class classification, producing misleading training gradients.

The authors empirically attribute the forgetting observed in that benchmark to its experimental design rather than inherent modeling limitations. This is a finding about the investigated setup, not an explanation for all catastrophic forgetting. They propose a more general NLP evaluation framework and build benchmarks spanning multiple domains, languages, and levels of linguistic hierarchy.

The framework separately targets properties such as forgetting and difficulty learning new tasks, and introduces Area Under the Lifelong Test Curve for continuous evaluation. Under the authors' realistic lifelong-learning setup, prevalent memory-based methods fail to outperform a simple experience replay baseline. The findings show how benchmark design can change conclusions about method effectiveness and provide a more structured basis for evaluating both retention and continued learning.
neurips-2021-towards-a-robust-experiment.tldr: The paper exposes a lifelong-learning benchmark artifact and introduces broader evaluations where prevalent memory-based methods do not beat simple experience replay.

paragraphs: VALUE evaluates video-and-language systems across a wider range of demands than a single dataset or task. It combines 11 datasets covering text-to-video retrieval, video question answering, and video captioning. The collection spans different genres, video lengths, dataset sizes, and difficulty levels to support evaluation of broader generalization.

The benchmark encourages systems to use both video frames and associated subtitles, and to share knowledge across tasks. The authors examine baseline methods with and without large-scale pretraining, studying how input channels, ways of combining information, and video representations affect results. These comparisons make the sources and organization of information explicit parts of the evaluation.

The study also investigates transfer between tasks and different multitask-learning settings. Its best model remains substantially below human performance, identifying considerable room for improvement within the benchmark. VALUE's contribution is therefore both a broad evaluation resource and an experimental examination of design choices. It offers a setting for assessing whether progress extends across video-and-language uses rather than being confined to one dataset.
neurips-2021-value-a-multi-task-benchmar.tldr: VALUE evaluates video-and-language models across 11 datasets and three tasks, revealing a substantial gap between its best model and human performance.

paragraphs: WaveFake addresses the detection of generated audio, an area the authors identify as receiving less attention than image deepfakes. The paper responds to potential harms from generative modeling by providing resources for studying audio detection. Its contribution combines background material, a dataset, and baseline implementations intended to make further research easier.

The dataset contains nine sample sets produced using five different network architectures and spans two languages. This gives researchers generated audio from several model architectures within a common resource. The accompanying introduction to audio signal-processing techniques helps explain the kinds of analysis relevant to working with these signals.

The authors also provide two baseline models adapted from the signal-processing community. These give practitioners concrete starting points for experimentation alongside the data. The paper's stated contribution is the creation of an accessible research foundation for audio deepfake detection: researchers receive examples to study, methods for analyzing audio, and initial detection approaches to build upon. The combination broadens the available infrastructure for investigating generated speech and other audio signals.
neurips-2021-wavefake-a-data-set-to-faci.tldr: WaveFake supports audio deepfake research with samples from five generative architectures, two languages, signal-processing guidance, and two baseline models.
